blocks.text: Paul addresses a reported case in which a man is living with his father’s wife. He rebukes the community’s pride, calls it to mourn, and directs communal action toward the man. The chapter’s concern is therefore both the reported conduct and the congregation’s response to it.

The report is brief and focuses its directive on the man. It does not tell the woman’s voice, status, consent, or fate, so those matters should not be filled in with speculation. Likewise, “deliver such a one unto Satan” is disciplinary language with an expressed aim of salvation, but its precise practice is unknown. The passage does not provide a complete case record.

Verses 9–13 qualify Paul’s instruction: he distinguishes people “within” the community from those outside it and says that avoiding all outsiders engaged in the listed conduct would require leaving the world. The instruction concerns a person identified as a sibling within the community, not a program of judging or withdrawing from outsiders indiscriminately.

Later references in 2 Corinthians to an offender and a painful conflict do not securely identify that offender with the man in this chapter. The two passages may be compared, but they should not be turned into a single reconstructed biography.

This distinction limits communal authority to its own voluntary, bounded setting. It resists treating the chapter’s discipline language as authorization for indiscriminate shunning, retaliation, or pressure that endangers a person’s essential needs. Any boundary must remain proportionate, reviewable, and distinct from broader social punishment.
